Yeah there was the odd exception here or there but by far and away, girls were not in to that stuff. A friend's mom would drop all the kids off at the mall. We'd go check out video games, girls would go check out clothes.

Nothing kept girls from doing the same things we were doing. But yeah, since they weren't, a lot of this stuff kind of came up in our image. Overwhelmingly so at times I'm sure. Take video games. In many ways it scratches the same itch for guys that sports do. It lets guys try to assert their dominance and take out their aggression. There's tons of trash talking, and not just to your opponents, but to your team mates as well. You gotta prove you can take it and dish it out and figure out your place in the group. If you tell a girl she looks like a dude, the reason it's insulting is because she doesn't want to look like a guy. I was on the internet at age 12-13 in the late 90’s, and there was no shortage of jerks then, but we were also constantly reminded that it was a place full of people you don’t know who are probably lying about everything. You generally weren’t interacting with anybody you knew offline, so who really gave a shit? To us, the internet was pretty much a different world that had no bearing on offline reality. (Except when mom kept disconnecting you by picking up the phone.)

However, nowadays with Facebook and other social media sites, a lot of people (especially teenagers) are interacting with the same people they know offline, which leads to a different dynamic. They don’t just go home from school and enter a different world full of entirely different people like I did, they’re continuing the same social interactions that they were dealing with all day. The division between online and offline is blurred so much anymore that even when they’re dealing with strangers, I don’t think they can disengage quite as well as those of us who were raised in Web 1.0 can.

I think the real issue here is that technology changed the social landscape so much in the last 10 years that it spawned a generation of kids who ill-equipped to handle it.
